hints: Recall how moles links to concentration and volume, and first convert the volume from $\text{cm}^3$ to $\text{dm}^3$ by dividing by 1000.
walkthrough:
Convert volume and apply moles equals concentration times volume**
You have $40.0 \text{ cm}^3$ of $1.00 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{HCl}$. Concentration is in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, so volume must be in $\text{dm}^3$. Divide by 1000: $$40.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 0.0400 \text{ dm}^3$$ Then: $$n = c \times V = 1.00 \times 0.0400 = 0.0400 \text{ mol}$$

hints: Think about what a carbonate plus an acid always makes, remembering that complete reaction of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ gives $\text{CO}_2$ plus water plus the salt.
walkthrough:
Build the products then balance**
Sodium carbonate is a base. With excess hydrochloric acid it is completely neutralised to the salt sodium chloride, carbon dioxide and water. Write the skeleton: $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ You need 2 $\text{Na}$ on the right, so 2 $\text{NaCl}$, and that needs 2 $\text{HCl}$ on the left. That balances everything: $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Focus only on the sodium carbonate used in the titration, convert $15.0 \text{ cm}^3$ to $\text{dm}^3$ and multiply by $0.050 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough:
Calculate moles of the known solution**
This is a straightforward $n = cV$ for $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$: $$V = 15.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 0.0150 \text{ dm}^3$$ $$n(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3) = 0.050 \times 0.0150 = 7.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$

hints: Look back at your equation in (b)(i) to find how many moles of $\text{HCl}$ react with one mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$.
walkthrough:
Use the 1 to 2 ratio to find HCl in the sample**
From (b)(i): $$1 \text{ mol Na}_2\text{CO}_3 : 2 \text{ mol HCl}$$ So double the answer from (b)(ii): $$n(\text{HCl}) = 2 \times 7.5 \times 10^{-4} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ This is the HCl present in just the $10.0 \text{ cm}^3$ pipetted sample.

hints: Remember the $10.0 \text{ cm}^3$ sample is only a fraction of the $100 \text{ cm}^3$ flask, so ask yourself what factor scales the sample up to the whole flask.
walkthrough:
Scale the aliquot up to the total solution**
The remaining acid was made up to $100 \text{ cm}^3$, but you only titrated $10.0 \text{ cm}^3$. That is one tenth of the total: $$\text{scaling factor} = \frac{100}{10.0} = 10$$ Multiply: $$n(\text{HCl remaining, total}) = 10 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3} = 1.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$$

hints: Picture the story: you started with the amount from (a), some was used by metal M, and the rest was left over in (b)(iv), so subtract to find what was used.
walkthrough:
Subtract leftover acid from starting acid**
Initial $\text{HCl} = 0.0400$ mol from (a). Leftover $\text{HCl} = 0.015$ mol from (b)(iv). The difference must have reacted with M: $$n(\text{HCl reacted}) = 0.0400 - 0.015 = 0.025 \text{ mol}$$

hints: Use equation 1, $\text{M} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MCl}_2 + \text{H}_2$, to relate moles of $\text{HCl}$ used to moles of M.
walkthrough:
Apply the metal to acid ratio**
Equation 1 shows: $$1 \text{ mol M} : 2 \text{ mol HCl}$$ You used $0.025$ mol $\text{HCl}$, so moles of M is half: $$n(\text{M}) = \frac{0.025}{2} = 0.0125 \text{ mol}$$

hints: Recall that $A_r$ links mass and moles by $M_r = mass \div moles$, using $0.50$ g and your answer from (vi).
Once you have a value near $40$, check which Group 2 metal has that relative atomic mass.
walkthrough:
Calculate $A_r$ from mass and moles**
You weighed $0.50$ g and found $0.0125$ mol of M: $$A_r = \frac{m}{n} = \frac{0.50}{0.0125} = 40$$

Match to the Group 2 metal**
A relative atomic mass of $40$ matches calcium, $\text{Ca}$, which is a Group 2 metal. That fits the $\text{MCl}_2$ formula in equation 1.
Final answer: $A_r$ of M $= \frac{0.50}{0.0125} = 40$; identity of M $=$ Ca / calcium
